newsitem.title: USA: Landmark Florida tobacco case may ride on science.
newsitem.headline: Landmark Florida tobacco case may ride on science.

text.p: A landmark lawsuit brought by U.S. flight attendants against the tobacco industry, confounded by sticky legal issues as it heads to trial, may ride on the science of secondhand smoke, experts say.

The class-action known as Broin v Philip Morris et al, will begin with jury selection Monday, six years after it was filed. It is the first secondhand smoke lawsuit and the first class-action against the industry to make it to trial.
The suit contends that some 60,000 flight attendants contracted a variety of ailments including lung cancer from breathing other people's cigarette smoke on passenger jets.

Getting the case to this point has been a trial in itself. The plaintiffs' lawyers, husband-and-wife legal team Susan and Stanley Rosenblatt, ran a gauntlet of industry challenges that included a battle royal to have the case certified as a class- action over the objections of the trial judge.
"We're in new and uncharted waters here," R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. deputy general counsel Daniel Donahue said. "There is a measure of uncertainty that we've never had before."
The Rosenblatts intend to argue that -- industry claims to the contrary -- scientists agree that inhaling tobacco smoke causes lung cancer, emphysema and other diseases.

"The industry has been brilliant at creating the image of a scientific controversy, when in fact there is a worldwide consensus," Stanley Rosenblatt said. "The only people standing on the other side is the tobacco companies."

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has declared environmental tobacco smoke a cause of cancer, and a recent report said Harvard University researchers found exposure to secondhand smoke nearly doubled the risk of heart disease.
But experts say the research on passive smoking is rather skimpy, and issues such as the chemical makeup of different types of environmental smoke muddy the waters.

"We're looking at exhaled smoke, not inhaled smoke. Then we're looking at sidestream smoke, which again is a different composition," said Jean Eggen, a law professor at the Widener University school of law in Wilmington, Delaware.

In addition to what it sees as the weakness of the scientific evidence, the industry believes the Rosenblatts will be hard pressed to prove the companies did anything wrong by making and selling a legal product.
"There's no legal basis for imposing financial penalties on an industry doing nothing more than what society says is OK," Donahue said.

The fact that the plaintiffs are non-smokers has stripped the tobacco companies of their time-tested defense, that the industry is not liable because smokers choose to smoke. It is a defense that has given big tobacco a nearly spotless record in four decades of litigation against smokers.
"The tobacco industry just can't say it's your fault for smoking," Eggen said. "And you can't say you should have quit your job. That's not a level of responsibility we want to assign to people."

In the absence of that defense, the Rosenblatts will try to make an emotional argument to jurors about what they claim is a decades-long attempt by industry executives to defraud the public by lying about the dangers of cigarettes.

Rosenblatt said he will make a broad appeal to the jurors' sense of right and wrong, pointing them to his depositions of company executives, in which he asks whether the labels on cigarettes -- warning of the health risks -- are true.
"They dance around the issue for as long as they can. But when they are ultimately required to answer the question, they say 'no.' he said. "I would hope that will make a jury angry."

Some experts believe the trial's structure ultimately may doom the case. In a two-stage trial, jurors will first hear evidence about the general causes of illness and the liability of the companies. In a second stage, individual plaintiffs will bid for compensation based on their own illnesses.

"Most state courts ... have held that you have to have at least some base of compensatory damages in order to decide punitive damages," Eggen said. "I do question whether that would stand up from a due process standpoint."
There is also lingering uncertainty over whether a case with thousands of plaintiffs suffering from two dozen different illnesses can be fairly tried as a class-action.
Dade County Judge Robert Kaye initially refused to certify the class, doing so only when ordered by an appeals court.
Melissa Ronan of Litigation Analysis for Wall Street said the lawsuit may eventually collapse under its own weight.
"There's no precedent for trying a class-action that involves this many people," she said. "I just think at some point the plaintiffs or the judge are going to give up."
